chapters.title: Periodic law, periods and blocks
chapters.formula: Atomic number organizes recurring electron patterns
chapters.script: Welcome to Periodic Trends. This recorded Chemistry class uses an AI generated Marin voice. The modern periodic law connects recurring properties with atomic number, not merely atomic mass. Increasing nuclear charge determines the electron count of a neutral atom, while recurring outer configurations explain many similarities. Period number usually identifies the highest occupied principal shell in a ground state main group atom. Sodium ends in three s one, placing it in period three and group one. Chlorine ends in three s two, three p five, placing it in period three and group seventeen. Electronic blocks describe the kind of subshell receiving the differentiating electron. Sodium is s block and chlorine is p block. Helium has one s two, so its configuration is s type, yet its closed shell chemistry places it in group eighteen with noble gases. Do not confuse electronic block with group placement. Transition and inner transition series require care because their filling subshells are not the outermost principal shell. Elements in the same group can still differ in their chemical reactions.
points: Na · 3s¹ · Period 3; group 1
Cl · 3s² 3p⁵ · Period 3; group 17
He · 1s² · Group 18; s-type

chapters.title: Shielding and effective attraction
chapters.formula: Nuclear attraction competes with shielding and shell size
chapters.script: An electron feels attraction to the nucleus and repulsion from other electrons. Effective nuclear charge is a model for the net nuclear attraction experienced by a particular electron after shielding is considered. It is not automatically atomic number minus every other electron: shielding effectiveness depends on orbital distribution. Inner electrons generally shield an outer electron more effectively than electrons in the same shell. Across a typical main group period, protons are added while electrons enter the same principal shell, so shielding does not fully cancel the increased nuclear charge. The outer cloud generally contracts. Down a group, additional occupied shells increase typical distance and shielding; the outer size generally grows despite more protons. Penetration also matters: within a shell, an s orbital samples regions nearer the nucleus more strongly than a p orbital in the usual qualitative comparison. This helps explain subshell energy differences in many electron atoms. Use these competing effects to explain a trend before memorizing an arrow. A qualitative effective charge argument is not a numerical calculation unless a specific model is supplied.
points: Across a period · More Z; same shell · Stronger attraction
Down a group · More occupied shells · Larger outer cloud
Same-shell orbitals · Different penetration · Different energies

chapters.title: Atomic and ionic radius comparisons
chapters.formula: Specify radius type before comparing values
chapters.script: Atomic radius is inferred from distances, so its definition matters. A covalent radius is commonly based on a bonded internuclear distance, while a van der Waals radius describes nonbonded contact. Metallic radii use distances in metallic structures. Do not compare a noble gas nonbonded radius with a neighbouring element's covalent radius and treat the difference as a simple exception to one identical measurement. Within a consistent set, main group atomic radii generally decrease across a period and increase down a group. A positive ion is usually smaller than its neutral parent because electrons are removed and attraction per remaining electron increases; losing an entire outer shell makes the contraction especially strong. A negative ion is usually larger because added electrons increase repulsion in the cloud. Sodium ion is smaller than sodium atom, whereas chloride ion is larger than chlorine atom. Ionic radius values also depend on coordination and the structural convention used to assign them. Always identify whether the question compares atoms, ions or an isoelectronic series before ranking sizes.
points: Na⁺ versus Na · Na⁺ smaller · Outer shell removed
Cl⁻ versus Cl · Cl⁻ larger · Added repulsion

chapters.title: Isoelectronic species and electron counts
chapters.formula: At equal electron count, larger Z contracts the cloud
chapters.script: Isoelectronic species have the same number of electrons. That common count makes nuclear charge a useful comparison, provided the species are being compared on a consistent basis. Oxygen two minus has eight protons and ten electrons. Fluoride has nine protons and ten electrons. Sodium plus has eleven protons and ten electrons, while magnesium two plus has twelve protons and ten electrons. The radius decreases in that order because increasing nuclear charge pulls the common electron population inward more strongly. Thus oxide is largest and magnesium two plus smallest in this set. Do the subtraction explicitly: electron count equals atomic number minus signed ionic charge. A negative charge therefore adds electrons. Do not compare raw charge labels without checking which element is involved. An ion with a larger positive charge is not automatically smaller than every other ion in the periodic table, because different occupied shells can dominate. For another ten electron member, aluminium three plus has thirteen protons and lies smaller than magnesium two plus in the same qualitative sequence. This reasoning concerns size, not which isolated ion is easiest to produce.

chapters.title: Ionization energies and familiar exceptions
chapters.formula: Gaseous X → X⁺ + e⁻ requires energy
chapters.script: First ionization energy removes one electron from an isolated gaseous atom in its ground state. It is positive for this process. Across a typical main group period it generally increases, and down a group it generally decreases, but electronic details produce important exceptions. Beryllium has a filled two s subshell, whereas boron loses its first two p electron. That higher energy, less penetrating electron is easier to remove, so beryllium has the larger first ionization energy. Nitrogen has three singly occupied two p orbitals. Oxygen introduces a pair into one of them, and removal of a paired electron relieves repulsion. Nitrogen therefore has the larger first ionization energy despite oxygen's greater nuclear charge. Similar reasoning helps with magnesium versus aluminium and phosphorus versus sulfur. These explanations refine the broad trend; they do not justify ignoring all nuclear attraction effects. Ionization energy is not the energy needed to break a chemical bond, nor the tendency to attract shared electrons. Write the gas phase electron removal process before deciding which quantity a question asks about.
points: Be versus B · Be · B loses a 2p electron
N versus O · N · O has a paired 2p e⁻
Mg versus Al · Mg · Al loses a 3p electron

board.heading: Ionization energies and familiar exceptions

chapters.title: Successive removal and valence patterns
chapters.formula: Large IE jump can reveal a stable inner core
chapters.script: Successive ionization energies refer to removing electrons one at a time from increasingly positive gaseous ions. The second removes an electron from a singly positive ion, not another fresh neutral atom. Successive removal generally costs more, and a particularly large jump can identify when an inner closed shell must be disrupted. Magnesium has a neon core followed by three s two. Removing two outer electrons gives the neon-like magnesium two plus ion. The third ionization then removes a core electron, so the major jump is between the second and third values. Sodium has only one outer three s electron and shows its core-related jump after the first removal. In simple main group comparisons this connects configurations with common ionic charges. However, oxidation state is formal electron bookkeeping in a compound, not proof that free ions with those charges exist. Chlorine often has minus one in chlorides but can have positive oxidation states in oxygen compounds; fluorine has minus one in its compounds. Group similarity does not mean a single allowed oxidation state for every member.
points: Na · 3s¹ · After first removal
Mg · 3s² · After second removal

chapters.title: Electron gain and electronegativity
chapters.formula: Electron gain enthalpy and bond attraction are different
chapters.script: For electron gain enthalpy, write a gaseous atom plus an electron forming a gaseous negative ion. If energy is released, the enthalpy change is negative under this convention. Some electron affinity tables instead report the positive magnitude of released energy. Read the sign convention before ordering values. Chlorine has a more negative first electron gain enthalpy than fluorine. Fluorine's compact two p electron cloud produces stronger repulsion for the incoming electron, so the simple expectation from atomic size alone fails. Adding a second electron to an already negative isolated gaseous ion requires energy because the incoming electron encounters repulsion. Formation of a stable ionic solid can still be favourable when the entire energy cycle, including lattice formation, is considered. Electronegativity is different: it describes an atom's attraction for shared electron density in a bond on a chosen scale. Fluorine is more electronegative than chlorine even though chlorine's first electron gain is more exothermic. Keep process energies, sign conventions and bond-based scales in separate columns.

chapters.title: Reactivity, oxides and trend limits
chapters.formula: Use trends with the stated reaction conditions
chapters.script: Metallic character generally decreases across a main group period and increases down a group. This supports broad changes in oxide behaviour. Across period three, sodium oxide and magnesium oxide are basic, aluminium oxide is amphoteric, and several nonmetal oxides are acidic. Amphoteric means reacting with both acids and bases under suitable conditions; it does not mean the oxide has no acid base chemistry. Do not extend a broad trend to every oxidation state or every oxide without checking the compound. Alkali metals generally become easier to ionize down the group, but a measured reaction depends on more than ionization alone. Hydration energies, bond breaking, physical state and kinetics can change comparisons. Halogen oxidizing strength in ordinary aqueous chemistry broadly decreases down the group, yet electron gain enthalpy by itself cannot supply the full explanation. For a ranking question, first identify the property, then compare configurations, shells and the relevant process. Finally inspect known exceptions and conditions. The practice questions combine those steps; further group chemistry and detailed transition element trends require separate study.
points: Na₂O; MgO · Basic · React with acids
Al₂O₃ · Amphoteric · Acids and bases
SO₃ · Acidic · Acid-forming oxide

chapters.title: Infer valence from a successive-energy jump
chapters.formula: Large jump after IEₖ suggests k outer electrons in a suitable main-group model
chapters.script: Successive ionization data can reveal a valence pattern when a much larger energy is required after the outer electrons have been removed. Take supplied values five hundred seventy eight, one thousand eight hundred seventeen, two thousand seven hundred forty five and eleven thousand five hundred seventy seven kilojoules per mole. The conspicuous jump is between the third and fourth removals. In a suitable main group interpretation this suggests three outer electrons before a more tightly bound inner shell is reached. It is consistent with group thirteen behaviour, but these four values alone are not a general proof of an exact atomic number. Each successive ionization starts from a different, more positively charged gaseous ion, so the terms are not repeated removals from an unchanged neutral atom. To form the triply charged gaseous ion from the neutral gaseous atom, add the first three energies, giving five thousand one hundred forty. Do not use only the third energy for the whole process. Configuration, periodic position and the stated model should support the assignment, especially when transition elements or unusual electronic states are possible.

chapters.title: Keep electron-gain energy signs explicit
chapters.formula: X(g) + e⁻ → X⁻(g): negative ΔH means energy release
chapters.script: Electron gain enthalpy describes the energy change when a gaseous species accepts an electron. Under the enthalpy change convention, an exothermic addition has a negative value. A table of electron affinity may instead report a positive magnitude for energy released, so the same physical event can appear with a different sign convention. Read the defining reaction and heading first. Suppose illustrative first electron gain enthalpies are minus three hundred twenty eight for fluorine and minus three hundred forty nine kilojoules per mole for chlorine. Chlorine releases more energy in this comparison, despite fluorine being higher in the group. The compact fluorine valence shell produces stronger repulsions for the added electron. Now distinguish adding an electron to a neutral oxygen atom from adding another to an oxygen anion. The second addition faces electrostatic repulsion and is endothermic for the isolated gaseous ion. The existence of oxide ions in solids does not contradict that fact: lattice formation and other steps contribute to the overall thermodynamic cycle. One electron gain term alone cannot decide whether an entire ionic compound forms.

chapters.title: Compare radii defined by the same method
chapters.formula: Covalent, metallic, van der Waals and ionic radii use different definitions
chapters.script: An atomic radius is an operational description, not a sharply defined surface around an electron cloud. A covalent radius can be obtained from half the internuclear distance between identical bonded atoms. If a supplied homonuclear single bond distance is one hundred ninety eight picometres, that convention gives ninety nine picometres for the atom. A van der Waals radius uses nonbonded contacts and is usually larger for the same element. Metallic and ionic radii come from other structural environments. An ionic radius also depends on the stated coordination and oxidation state convention. Therefore a ranking that mixes a noble gas van der Waals value with a neighbour's covalent value can produce an apparent exception that reflects the measurement definition. Within a consistent isoelectronic series, increasing nuclear charge commonly contracts the electronic distribution; within one element, a cation is generally smaller than its neutral atom under suitable comparisons. These useful trends do not remove the need to compare compatible datasets. Check charge, electron count, coordination environment and radius definition before explaining a small numerical difference as a new periodic law.

chapters.title: Use oxide equations to support classification
chapters.formula: Amphoteric oxides react with both acids and bases under suitable conditions
chapters.script: Oxide acid base classification should be supported by the actual compound and a balanced reaction. Sodium oxide reacts with hydrochloric acid to form sodium chloride and water: one sodium oxide requires two hydrogen chloride units. Aluminium oxide can react with acid as well. One aluminium oxide plus six hydrogen chloride units forms two aluminium chloride units and three waters in a simplified formula equation. Under suitable aqueous strongly basic conditions, aluminium oxide can form tetrahydroxoaluminate. A balanced representation uses one aluminium oxide, two hydroxide ions and three waters to form two tetrahydroxoaluminate ions. This acid and base behaviour supports the word amphoteric. It does not mean the oxide is neutral or reacts equally rapidly under arbitrary conditions. Silicon dioxide can show acidic oxide behaviour through reactions with suitable strong bases, while conditions and product conventions must be stated. Oxidation state matters too: different oxides of the same element need not share one classification. Use a broad across period trend to organize examples, then check the actual chemistry rather than treating a left to right arrow as a substitute for an equation.

Al₂O₃ + 6HCl · → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O · Reaction with acid
Al₂O₃ + 2OH⁻ + 3H₂O · → 2[Al(OH)₄]⁻ · Reaction with base

chapters.title: Aqueous reducing power needs the full process
chapters.formula: More negative standard reduction potential can indicate a stronger reverse reducing tendency
chapters.script: A gas phase ionization trend does not by itself determine the reducing strength of a metal in aqueous standard conditions. Converting a solid metal to an aqueous cation involves atomization, ionization and hydration contributions. Compare the supplied standard reduction potentials for lithium, sodium and potassium ions becoming their metals: minus three point zero four, minus two point seven one and minus two point nine three volts respectively. Reversing each half reaction describes metal oxidation. In this comparison lithium has the most negative reduction potential and the strongest standard thermodynamic reducing tendency of the three metals. This does not follow the simple expectation obtained by looking only at how easily a gas phase electron is removed down the group. Strong stabilization of the small aqueous lithium ion is part of the explanation. These potentials do not rank the observed speed or violence of a metal reacting with water. Surface condition, melting, mass transfer and reaction pathways affect that observation. Keep thermodynamic tendency, individual energy terms and reaction rate distinct. Use the stated solvent and standard conditions; changing the medium can change the comparison.

chapters.title: Locate an element from a main-group configuration
chapters.formula: [Ne]3s²3p³: period 3, group 15, p block
chapters.script: An electron configuration can locate a neutral main group atom when the subshell pattern is read carefully. Consider a supplied configuration with a neon core, two electrons in three s and three in three p. The largest occupied principal quantum number is three, so this atom lies in period three. Five electrons occupy the outer s and p subshells together, giving group fifteen in the usual main group numbering. The differentiating electron enters a p subshell, so it is a p block element. The total electron count is ten plus two plus three, or fifteen; for the neutral atom the atomic number is also fifteen. Do not identify group three merely from the superscript on the p subshell, and do not identify the period from the number of valence electrons. An ion requires another step: the configuration describes its remaining electrons, not necessarily the neutral parent atomic number. Helium is a familiar boundary case, with a filled one s shell but placement in group eighteen based on the periodic organization. The simple s and p group shortcut should not be extended unchanged to transition metal configurations.

chapters.title: Isotopes share a periodic position because Z is unchanged
chapters.formula: Atomic number counts protons; isotope mass does not set a new group
chapters.script: The modern periodic table organizes elements by atomic number, not by assigning a separate chemical position to each isotope mass. Consider chlorine thirty five and chlorine thirty seven, both with seventeen protons. Neutral atoms of each have seventeen electrons, giving the same ordinary electron configuration pattern and the same periodic group and period. Their neutron counts differ: eighteen for mass number thirty five and twenty for mass number thirty seven. A chloride ion has one extra electron, eighteen in total, but its nucleus still has seventeen protons. It remains chlorine rather than turning into argon, whose nucleus has eighteen protons. Thus isotope formation, ion formation and changing the element are distinct operations. Chemical properties of isotopes are similar because of their electronic structures, though isotope effects mean they are not identical in every measurable process. Mass number is the integer proton plus neutron count for a specified nuclide, while relative atomic mass of a natural sample is an isotopic average. Reading an average near thirty five point five as an individual atom with a fractional neutron count would confuse these two quantities. Always identify charge and nuclide information before counting electrons or locating the element.

chapters.title: Two electron-gain steps need separate energy signs
chapters.formula: O(g) + 2e⁻ → O²⁻(g): sum both supplied step energies
chapters.script: The energy of adding a second electron cannot be copied from the first electron gain. For an isolated gas phase oxygen atom, the first addition makes an anion, whereas the second addition brings another negative electron toward an already negative ion. The second step is generally energetically costly for forming such a multiply charged isolated anion. Use supplied illustrative step values of minus one hundred forty one and plus seven hundred forty four kilojoules per mole for the first and second oxygen electron additions. The total energy change for forming gas phase oxide ions from gas phase oxygen atoms and two electrons is plus six hundred three kilojoules per mole. Thus the complete two electron gas phase process is endothermic under those supplied values even though the first step is exothermic. This does not mean oxide solids cannot be stable. Formation of a solid includes other contributions, especially favourable lattice formation, and any full formation calculation also needs the appropriate atomization and metal ionization steps. Keep the isolated ion process distinct from the complete solid formation cycle. State whether a quoted electron affinity uses an energy released convention or an electron gain enthalpy convention before attaching a sign.

chapters.title: Supporting conversion: molar ionization energy and photons
chapters.formula: 1 eV per particle = 96.485 kJ/mol; E(eV) ≈ 1240/λ(nm)
chapters.script: As a supporting connection to atomic energy calculations, convert an ionization energy without mixing particle and mole units. Suppose a hypothetical isolated gas phase atom has first ionization threshold five point zero zero electron volts per atom. With the supplied conversion one electron volt per particle equals ninety six point four eight five kilojoules per mole, the molar threshold is four hundred eighty two point four two five kilojoules per mole. That number is not the energy of one individual atom in kilojoules. For a photon comparison, use the supplied relation photon energy in electron volts equals approximately twelve hundred forty divided by wavelength in nanometres. A threshold of five electron volts corresponds to about two hundred forty eight nanometres. A two hundred nanometre photon has about six point two electron volts, exceeding this ideal threshold, whereas a three hundred nanometre photon has about four point one three and is below it. These are energy comparisons for the stipulated one photon isolated atom model, not predictions of an experimental ionization yield. Cross sections, states and experimental conditions matter. chapters.title: Selected diagonal similarities need actual compounds
chapters.formula: Li/Mg: Li₃N and Mg₃N₂; Be/Al: selected amphoteric oxide behaviour
chapters.script: A diagonal relationship is a selected chemical similarity between elements in different groups, not a claim that their electron configurations are identical. Lithium and magnesium are a familiar supporting comparison: both can form nitrides by direct combination with nitrogen under suitable conditions. Lithium nitride is lithium three N, whereas magnesium nitride is magnesium three N two. Their formulas follow lithium plus one, magnesium plus two and nitride minus three charge bookkeeping. In ideal hydrolysis equations, one lithium nitride with three waters gives three lithium hydroxides and one ammonia. One magnesium nitride with six waters gives three magnesium hydroxides and two ammonias. Equal formula unit amounts therefore produce different ammonia amounts. Beryllium and aluminium supply another selected diagonal comparison because their oxides can show amphoteric behaviour. This is resemblance in particular chemistry, not interchangeability of every salt, reaction condition or oxidation state. Small sizes and charge density help organize these patterns, but a simple diagonal arrow cannot replace balanced equations. These examples support periodic reasoning; they do not imply that every historical s block preparation belongs to the current syllabus or that all neighbouring diagonal pairs behave identically.

chapters.title: Hydride acidity needs direction and bond strength
chapters.formula: Across Period 2: CH₄ < NH₃ < H₂O < HF in proton-donation tendency; aqueous HCl stronger than HF
chapters.script: Electronegativity helps organize some acid strength trends, but it is not the only variable. Across the simple second period hydrogen compounds, the qualitative proton donation tendency increases from methane through ammonia and water to hydrogen fluoride. Increasing attraction for electron density helps stabilize the negative species left after proton loss. This compares the acid role of each hydride; ammonia can still be a base in an ordinary reaction with water or an acid. Down a group, changing atom size and bond strength can outweigh the electronegativity trend. Hydrogen chloride is a strong acid in ordinary dilute water, whereas hydrogen fluoride is a weak acid even though fluorine is more electronegative. The particularly strong hydrogen fluorine bond is part of the explanation; solution stabilization must also be included in a full thermodynamic account. Do not confuse this hydrogen halide bond comparison with the fluorine fluorine bond in elemental fluorine. Solvent matters, and water levels several strong acids by converting them substantially to hydronium. A periodic arrow therefore helps form a hypothesis, but the actual species, solvent and proton transfer equilibrium decide the comparison.

chapters.title: Period 3 melting points follow structures, not one arrow
chapters.formula: Na/Mg/Al: metallic; Si: covalent network; white P₄, S₈, Cl₂: molecular; Ar: monatomic
chapters.script: A melting point trend across a period must be connected to the structures actually present. Sodium, magnesium and aluminium are metallic solids, with different metallic interactions and crystal structures. Silicon instead has an extended covalent network, so melting requires major disruption of a connected bonding framework. Its high melting point cannot be explained by imagining separate silicon molecules held together only by weak dispersion forces. On the right side, specify the allotrope: white phosphorus contains P four molecules, ordinary molecular sulfur contains S eight rings, and chlorine consists of chlorine two molecules. Their solid structures involve attractions between those molecules. Solid argon contains individual atoms held by dispersion forces, not argon two molecules or a covalent network. Molecular size, polarizability and packing contribute to differences between the molecular solids. Melting does not normally mean breaking every covalent bond within each phosphorus or sulfur molecule. Nor does atomic number alone enforce a steady increase or decrease in melting point across the period. Use the stated elemental form, pressure and bonding category before comparing a property, and do not transfer the white phosphorus description to every phosphorus allotrope.

chapters.title: The short fluorine bond is a strength exception
chapters.formula: Supplied gas-phase D(F₂)=158 and D(Cl₂)=243 kJ/mol; atomization per mol atoms is D/2
chapters.script: A shorter homonuclear bond is not automatically stronger when comparing different elements. Elemental fluorine has a short fluorine fluorine bond, yet its dissociation enthalpy is lower than that of chlorine chlorine. In the usual qualitative explanation, the small fluorine atoms bring nonbonding electron pairs close together, and their repulsions weaken the bond. This does not mean that every bond containing fluorine is weak: the hydrogen fluorine bond is especially strong. For a numerical comparison, take supplied representative gas phase dissociation enthalpies of one hundred fifty eight kilojoules per mole fluorine molecules and two hundred forty three per mole chlorine molecules. Dissociating one mole of either diatomic produces two moles of atoms. The corresponding enthalpy per mole of atoms is therefore seventy nine for fluorine and one hundred twenty one point five for chlorine. Confusing a mole of molecules with a mole of atoms introduces a factor of two error. Bond dissociation alone also cannot rank all aqueous oxidizing strengths, because electron gain, solvation and other steps contribute. Specify the bond, physical state and amount basis before turning a periodic size trend into an energy prediction.

chapters.title: Oxide, peroxide and superoxide contain different oxygen species
chapters.formula: Li₂O: O²⁻; Na₂O₂: O₂²⁻; KO₂: O₂⁻; oxygen oxidation numbers −2, −1, −½
chapters.script: Similar looking oxygen formulas can represent different anions. Lithium oxide contains an oxide ion, one oxygen atom with charge minus two. Sodium peroxide contains a peroxide unit, two oxygens sharing total charge minus two. Potassium superoxide contains a superoxide unit, two oxygens sharing total charge minus one. With the metal assigned plus one, oxygen oxidation numbers are therefore minus two, minus one and minus one half, respectively. The fractional superoxide value is an average oxidation number, not a claim that an isolated oxygen atom has half an electron attached. An oxide ion has ten total electrons; peroxide and superoxide molecular ions have eighteen and seventeen, respectively. In the elementary isolated oxygen ion orbital model, peroxide has all electrons paired whereas superoxide has one unpaired electron. This connects charge bookkeeping to magnetic predictions without confusing an atomic ion with a two atom ion. These named compounds illustrate selected size and charge density trends in alkali metal chemistry. Actual oxygen reaction products depend on conditions and can include mixtures, so do not turn this illustrative sequence into a guarantee that each metal forms only one oxygen compound under every circumstance.

KO₂: one O₂⁻ unit · Each O: −½; unit has 17 e⁻ · One unpaired e⁻ in elementary model

chapters.title: Halogen displacement follows the specified oxidizing comparison
chapters.formula: E°cell=E°(halogen reduced)−E°(halide oxidized); Cl₂+2Br⁻→2Cl⁻+Br₂
chapters.script: A periodic oxidizing trend becomes a testable electron transfer comparison when both half reactions are specified. Use supplied standard reduction potentials one point three six volts for chlorine to chloride, one point zero seven for bromine to bromide and zero point five four for iodine accepting electrons to form the anion I minus. Chlorine accepting electrons while bromide loses them gives cell potential one point three six minus one point zero seven, or plus zero point two nine volt. The balanced net reaction is one chlorine molecule plus two bromides forming two chlorides and one bromine molecule. Bromine accepting electrons from iodide anions, written I minus, similarly gives plus zero point five three volt. Iodine oxidizing chloride instead gives zero point five four minus one point three six, or minus zero point eight two volt, so that written direction is not standard thermodynamically favoured in this comparison. Chlorine, bromine and iodine therefore form the stated descending oxidizing sequence. Equal amounts of gas and salt are not generally the reaction ratio: one mole halogen consumes two moles monovalent halide. These standard state predictions do not specify reaction speed or replace concentration and solvent checks. Fluorine's reaction with water prevents treating it as an interchangeable ordinary aqueous displacement test.

chapters.title: Group 2 hydroxides and sulfates do not share one solubility arrow
chapters.formula: For M(OH)₂ in the stated ideal pure-water model: Ksp=[M²⁺][OH⁻]²=4s³
chapters.script: A group trend must name the anion as well as the metal. From magnesium toward barium, hydroxide solubility generally increases, while sulfate solubility generally decreases in the usual aqueous comparison. There is no single rule saying that every salt becomes more soluble down this group. Lattice separation, hydration and entropy all contribute to dissolution free energy, and their balance depends on the compound. Use an explicitly ideal pure water calculation for a divalent metal hydroxide, excluding complexation, hydrolysis and water's small background contribution. If its molar solubility is s, dissolved metal concentration is s and hydroxide concentration twice s, giving solubility product four s cubed. With supplied illustrative barium hydroxide constant two point five six times ten to the minus four, the model solubility is zero point zero four zero zero molar. A supplied magnesium hydroxide constant one point zero eight times ten to the minus eleven gives about one point three nine times ten to the minus four molar under that same model. These concentration based results are not promises of exact measured values when activity effects become appreciable. Do not reuse a one to one salt's square root formula for this hydroxide stoichiometry.

chapters.title: Carbonate stability needs the cation and carbon dioxide pressure
chapters.formula: MCO₃(s) ⇌ MO(s)+CO₂(g); Li₂CO₃(s) ⇌ Li₂O(s)+CO₂(g)
chapters.script: Thermal stability describes a tendency under specified conditions, not a universal temperature printed on a formula. Magnesium to barium carbonates generally become harder to decompose in the usual group comparison. The smaller divalent cation polarizes carbonate more strongly, a useful qualitative contribution to this pattern. Lithium carbonate is less thermally stable than the other familiar alkali metal carbonates and can form lithium oxide plus carbon dioxide under appropriate conditions. This selected exception does not make lithium divalent; its decomposition equation contains lithium two carbonate and lithium two oxide, both with lithium plus one. Carbon dioxide pressure also matters. For a divalent carbonate in equilibrium with its oxide, when both pure solids are present, the equilibrium quotient involves carbon dioxide pressure relative to its standard pressure. Increasing that pressure opposes the decomposition direction at fixed temperature. In a supplied complete calcium carbonate decomposition ledger, five point zero zero grams with molar mass one hundred gives zero point zero five zero zero mole carbon dioxide. Its mass is two point two zero grams, leaving two point eight zero grams calcium oxide. The complete conversion ledger is a stipulated endpoint, not a prediction that a closed sample must fully decompose at any temperature.

quiz.question: The modern periodic law is based on:
quiz.explanation: Atomic number determines the nuclear charge and electronic pattern underlying periodic properties.

quiz.question: Which is smallest in the listed ten-electron series?
quiz.explanation: Mg2+ has the largest nuclear charge while all four species retain ten electrons.

quiz.question: Which exception to a simple increasing first-ionization trend is correct?
quiz.explanation: B loses a 2p electron more readily than Be loses a 2s electron, so Be has the higher value.

quiz.question: For exothermic X(g) + e- -> X-(g), electron gain enthalpy is:
quiz.explanation: The system releases energy, so its enthalpy change is negative under this stated convention.

quiz.question: A [Ne]3s2 atom has the largest core-related jump after removal of:
quiz.explanation: Two outer electrons are removed before ionization starts removing the neon-like core.

quiz.question: Which comparison is correct?
options: Fluorine has lower electronegativity than chlorine
Second electron gain is always exothermic
Chlorine's first electron gain enthalpy is more negative than fluorine's
quiz.explanation: Compact fluorine 2p orbitals create stronger added-electron repulsion; this does not reverse electronegativity.

quiz.question: Helium has configuration 1s2 but is placed in:
quiz.explanation: Its closed-shell chemistry places helium with the noble gases in group 18.

quiz.question: Which radius comparison is normally valid?
quiz.explanation: Sodium loses its outer shell on forming Na+, producing a smaller ion.

quiz.question: Which period-three oxide is amphoteric?
quiz.explanation: Aluminium oxide reacts with both acids and bases under suitable conditions.

quiz.question: Which is smaller within the same ten-electron series?
quiz.explanation: Both have ten electrons; Al3+ has the greater nuclear charge and smaller radius.

quiz.question: Successive IE data 578, 1817, 2745, 11577 kJ/mol show the major jump after removal number:
quiz.explanation: The largest jump is from IE3 to IE4, consistent with three outer electrons in the stated main-group model.

quiz.question: Using those data, energy for M(g) → M3+(g) + 3e− is:
With electron-gain enthalpies F=−328 and Cl=−349 kJ/mol, chlorine releases:
quiz.explanation: The chlorine step is 21 kJ/mol more exothermic under this enthalpy-change convention.

quiz.question: A supplied homonuclear single-bond distance of 198 pm gives covalent radius:
quiz.explanation: The same-atom covalent radius convention takes half the internuclear distance.

quiz.question: In Al2O3 + aOH− + bH2O → 2[Al(OH)4]−, the balanced values (a,b) are:
quiz.explanation: Two hydroxides conserve charge −2, and three waters complete the oxygen and hydrogen balance.

quiz.question: Given E°red Li=−3.04, Na=−2.71 and K=−2.93 V, which metal has strongest standard aqueous reducing tendency in this comparison?
options: All reaction speeds must be equal
quiz.explanation: Li has the most negative reduction potential of the supplied three; observed reaction rate is a separate issue.

quiz.question: Neutral [Ne]3s2 3p3 is in which period and group?
quiz.explanation: Largest occupied n gives period three; five outer s+p electrons give main group fifteen.

quiz.question: The neutral atomic number for that configuration is:
quiz.explanation: The neon core has ten electrons and the outer subshells add five; a neutral atom has the same proton count.

quiz.question: 35Cl and 37Cl share a periodic position because they share:
quiz.explanation: Isotopes of one element have the same proton count and ordinary neutral electron configuration pattern.

quiz.question: A 37Cl− ion has proton, neutron and electron counts:
quiz.explanation: Protons=17; neutrons=37−17=20; one negative charge gives 18 electrons.

quiz.question: O first and second electron-gain energies are supplied as −141 and +744 kJ/mol. Their sum is:
quiz.explanation: Add the sequential energy changes with signs: −141+744=+603 kJ/mol.

quiz.question: That endothermic isolated-ion sum means:
options: Every oxide solid must be unstable
The first electron gain was endothermic
A full solid-formation cycle needs other energy contributions
quiz.explanation: Isolated gas-phase ion formation is only part of a cycle; lattice, atomization and ionization terms also matter.

quiz.question: With 1 eV per particle = 96.485 kJ/mol, a 5.00 eV ionization threshold equals:
quiz.explanation: Multiply the per-particle electron-volt value by the supplied molar conversion.

quiz.question: Using E(eV)=1240/λ(nm), the wavelength corresponding to 5.00 eV is:
quiz.explanation: Solve λ=1240/5.00=248 nm for the supplied ideal photon-energy relation.

quiz.question: Which pair is the familiar selected diagonal relationship involving lithium?
quiz.explanation: Lithium and magnesium share selected compound-level similarities despite being in different groups.

quiz.question: Ideal hydrolysis of 0.0100 mol Mg3N2 gives how much NH3?
quiz.explanation: Each Mg3N2 formula unit contains two nitride nitrogen atoms and gives two ammonia molecules in the balanced model.

quiz.question: The standard qualitative increasing acid tendency across the simple second-period hydrides is:
quiz.explanation: Across this series electronegativity and stabilization of the conjugate negative species support increasing proton-donation tendency.

quiz.question: Why does fluorine electronegativity alone not make HF stronger than HCl in ordinary dilute water?
options: H–F bond strength and solution energetics also enter acid dissociation
Electronegativity and acid strength are identical quantities
quiz.explanation: The strong H–F bond matters, and a complete account includes solution stabilization; HCl is strong while HF is weak in this setting.

quiz.question: The appropriate structural explanation for silicon’s high melting point is:
options: A metallic free-electron sea identical to sodium
quiz.explanation: Silicon has an extended covalent framework, so major network disruption is involved in melting.

quiz.question: Which statement uses the correct elemental forms in the usual Period 3 comparison?
options: Every phosphorus allotrope contains discrete P4
Argon forms an Ar2 covalent network
White phosphorus contains P4; molecular sulfur contains S8
quiz.explanation: The allotrope and molecular form must be specified; white phosphorus and molecular sulfur have different molecular building units.

quiz.question: Given D(F2)=158 kJ per mol molecules, enthalpy to form one mol gaseous F atoms from F2(g) is:
quiz.explanation: One mole F2 forms two moles atoms, so atomization per mole atoms is half the molecular dissociation enthalpy.

quiz.question: Which statement correctly treats the F–F bond-strength exception?
options: All fluorine-containing bonds must be weak
F–F can be weaker than Cl–Cl despite being shorter
Shorter bonds between different elements are always stronger
F2 bond dissociation alone fixes every aqueous redox comparison
quiz.explanation: Compact lone-pair repulsions contribute to weak F–F bonding; bond identity and the full process must be kept distinct.

quiz.question: Oxygen oxidation numbers in Li₂O, Na₂O₂ and KO₂ are respectively:
quiz.explanation: Assign each alkali metal +1, then distinguish the oxide atom, peroxide pair and superoxide pair when balancing total charge.

quiz.question: Within the elementary isolated oxygen-ion model, which named compound contains the oxygen unit with one unpaired electron?
options: All three necessarily have identical oxygen-ion occupancy
quiz.explanation: KO₂ contains the 17-electron superoxide ion O₂⁻; peroxide has 18 and is paired in this elementary model.

quiz.question: Given E°(Cl₂/Cl⁻)=1.36 V and E°(Br₂/Br⁻)=1.07 V, E° for Cl₂+2Br⁻→2Cl⁻+Br₂ is:
quiz.explanation: Subtract the bromine reduction potential from the chlorine reduction potential; multiplying reaction coefficients does not multiply electrode potentials.

quiz.question: Complete ideal displacement of excess bromide by .0100 mol Cl₂ consumes bromide amount:
quiz.explanation: One chlorine molecule accepts two electrons from two bromide ions, so the bromide amount is twice the chlorine amount.

quiz.question: If M(OH)₂ alone dissolves to molar solubility s under the stated ideal model, its Ksp is:
quiz.explanation: Metal concentration is s and hydroxide is 2s; multiply s by (2s)², retaining the hydroxide exponent.

quiz.question: For supplied Ksp=2.56×10⁻⁴ in that M(OH)₂ model, molar solubility is:
quiz.explanation: s=(Ksp/4)^(1/3)=(6.40×10⁻⁵)^(1/3)=.0400 M under the specified concentration approximation.

quiz.question: Five grams pure CaCO₃ fully decompose in a stipulated endpoint model. With molar masses CaCO₃=100, CO₂=44 and CaO=56 g/mol, residue mass is:
quiz.explanation: The starting .0500 mol forms .0500 mol CaO, giving .0500×56=2.80 g; the missing 2.20 g is CO₂.

quiz.question: For MCO₃(s)⇌MO(s)+CO₂(g) with both pure solids present, adding CO₂ at fixed temperature tends to:
options: Change the equilibrium constant solely by adding gas
Turn lithium into a divalent metal
quiz.explanation: The gas activity raises the reaction quotient; the equilibrium response favours carbonate relative to the stated decomposition direction.
